q: In 1911, Heike Kamerlingh Onnes discovered this phenomenon in mercury cooled with liquid helium. Below a critical temperature, a material in this state has zero electrical resistance and expels magnetic fields, as described by the Meissner effect. MRI machines use magnets made of this. For 10 points, name this state of matter, which requires very low temperatures in conventional examples.

Doping with phosphorus makes these materials n-type, while doping with boron makes them p-type. Silicon and germanium are the most common examples. Their conductivity lies between that of a metal and an insulator and increases with temperature. For 10 points, name these materials, used to build diodes and transistors.

Scottish botanist Robert Brown first noticed this phenomenon in 1827 while watching pollen grains in water. Einstein's 1905 analysis of it explained the random jitter as collisions with invisible molecules, and Jean Perrin confirmed it experimentally. For 10 points, name this random motion of microscopic particles suspended in a fluid.

This theoretical engine was proposed in 1824 by a French engineer who showed that no heat engine operating between two temperatures can be more efficient than a reversible one. Its efficiency is one minus the ratio of the cold to hot reservoir temperatures in kelvin. For 10 points, name this idealized cycle, named for Sadi.

This German physicist introduced the idea that energy is emitted in discrete packets to explain blackbody radiation in 1900. The packet's energy equals frequency times a constant that bears his name. He won the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics. For 10 points, name this founder of quantum theory.

This is the rotational analog of mass. It equals the sum of each particle's mass times the square of its distance from the axis. A figure skater spins faster when she pulls in her arms because it decreases. For 10 points, name this quantity, which is smaller for a solid cylinder than a hollow one of the same mass and radius.

This English polymath performed a double-slit experiment around 1801 that showed light behaves as a wave. He also names a measure of the stiffness of materials and helped decipher the Rosetta Stone. For 10 points, name this physician and physicist.
Answer these questions about quantities used to describe motion.
parts: What term describes a quantity that has both magnitude and direction, like velocity?
What term describes a quantity that has magnitude only, like mass or temperature?
What is the name for the single quantity that results from combining several such quantities by addition?

q: Answer these questions about waves.
parts: Sound waves are which type of wave, in which particles of the medium vibrate parallel to the direction of travel?
What name is given to the points of zero displacement on a standing wave?
To the nearest ten meters per second, what is the speed of sound in air at room temperature?

q: Answer these questions about pioneers of electricity.
parts: Which Italian physicist invented the electric battery, the voltaic pile?
Which American founding father is said to have flown a kite in a thunderstorm to investigate lightning?
Which Serbian-American engineer developed the alternating-current induction motor?

q: Answer these questions about thermodynamics.
parts: What temperature scale, with units named for Lord Kelvin's title, starts at absolute zero?
What law of thermodynamics states that energy is conserved, with the change in internal energy equal to heat added minus work done?
What non-SI unit of heat is the energy needed to warm one gram of water by one degree Celsius?

q: Answer these questions about optics.
parts: What device produces an intense, coherent beam of light through stimulated emission?
What is the distance from a lens to its focal point called?
What kind of image, which cannot be projected on a screen, is formed by a plane mirror?

q: Answer these questions about the discovery of radiation and the nucleus.
parts: Which German physicist discovered X-rays in 1895?
Which French physicist discovered radioactivity in uranium salts in 1896?
Which English physicist discovered the neutron in 1932?

q: Answer these questions about Newtonian mechanics.
parts: Which law of motion states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction?
What kind of collision conserves both momentum and kinetic energy?
What kind of collision has the colliding objects stick together after impact?

q: Answer these questions about particle physics.
parts: What European laboratory near Geneva operates the Large Hadron Collider?
Which particle, whose discovery was announced in 2012, is associated with the field that gives mass to elementary particles?
What fundamental particles, which come in flavors like up and down, make up protons and neutrons?

q: Eugene Parker predicted this phenomenon in 1958. It is a stream of charged particles, mostly protons and electrons, that flows outward from the Sun's corona. It pushes the ion tails of comets away from the Sun and triggers auroras on Earth. For 10 points, name this flow of plasma.

This comet returns to the inner solar system about every 76 years. An English astronomer who predicted its return in 1758 gave it his name. It appears in the Bayeux Tapestry and passed near Earth in 1986. For 10 points, name this comet, which will be visible again in 2061.

Located in the constellation Canis Major, this is the brightest star in the night sky as seen from Earth. It is also called the Dog Star. It has a faint white dwarf companion. For 10 points, name this star, which ancient Egyptians connected with the flooding of the Nile.

This is the largest moon in the solar system, larger than the planet Mercury. It orbits Jupiter and has its own magnetic field. It was discovered by Galileo in 1610 along with three other large moons. For 10 points, name this moon.

This shield volcano on Mars rises about 22 kilometers above its surroundings, which makes it the tallest known volcano in the solar system. Its base is roughly as wide as the state of Arizona. For 10 points, name this Martian mountain, whose name means "Mount" of a Greek god's home.

In 1983, this physicist became the first American woman in space when she flew on the space shuttle Challenger. She later served on the panels investigating both the Challenger and Columbia disasters. For 10 points, name this astronaut.

This imaginary great circle on the celestial sphere traces the Sun's apparent yearly path among the stars. It is the projection of Earth's orbital plane. The zodiac constellations lie along it, and the Moon and planets always appear near it. For 10 points, name this line.

Earth reaches this point in its orbit in early January, when it is about 147 million kilometers from the Sun. It is the closest point in a body's orbit to the Sun. It is opposite aphelion. For 10 points, name this orbital point.

This red dwarf is the closest known star to the Sun at about 4.2 light-years. It is part of the Alpha Centauri system. It is too dim to be seen without a telescope, and it hosts at least one planet in its habitable zone. For 10 points, name this star.

Launched in 1977, this NASA spacecraft took the "Pale Blue Dot" photograph of Earth in 1990. It carries a golden phonograph record with sounds and images of Earth. It crossed into interstellar space in 2012. For 10 points, name this probe, the most distant human-made object.

This Danish nobleman made the most accurate naked-eye measurements of planetary positions from his observatory Uraniborg. He recorded the supernova of 1572 and lost part of his nose in a duel. His assistant Johannes Kepler used his data. For 10 points, name this astronomer.

This American astronomer used Cepheid variables at Mount Wilson to show in the 1920s that Andromeda lies far beyond the Milky Way. His law states that the recession speed of galaxies is proportional to their distance. For 10 points, name this man, for whom an orbiting telescope is named.

This plot shows luminosity or absolute magnitude of stars against temperature or spectral type. Most stars lie along a diagonal band across it, with red giants above and white dwarfs below. It is named for a Danish and an American astronomer. For 10 points, name this diagram.

Stars spend most of their lives in this stage, during which they fuse hydrogen into helium in their cores. The Sun will remain in it for roughly ten billion years in total. A star's position in it depends on its mass. For 10 points, name this longest stage of stellar evolution.

This is a dense stellar remnant left after the core of a massive star collapses in a supernova. It has about one and a half times the mass of the Sun packed into a sphere roughly 20 kilometers across. It is held up by neutron degeneracy pressure. For 10 points, name this object, a type of compact star.

Fritz Zwicky inferred this substance in the 1930s from the motions of galaxies in the Coma Cluster. Vera Rubin found that galaxies rotate too fast for their visible mass alone. It does not emit or absorb light. For 10 points, name this invisible form of matter that makes up much of the mass of the universe.

This is relic radiation from about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, when the universe first became transparent. It has a blackbody temperature of about 2.7 kelvin. It was discovered accidentally in 1964 using a horn antenna in New Jersey. For 10 points, name this faint glow that fills the sky at microwave frequencies.

This phenomenon is the stretching of light to longer wavelengths as a source moves away or as space expands. Vesto Slipher first measured it in spiral nebulae. Edwin Hubble used it to show that the universe is expanding. For 10 points, name this effect, which shifts light toward the long-wavelength end of the visible spectrum.

In 1995, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz discovered the first of these around a Sun-like star, 51 Pegasi b. NASA's Kepler telescope found thousands using the transit method. Astronomers also detect them by the wobble they induce in their star. For 10 points, name these planets that orbit stars other than the Sun.

This Greek astronomer wrote the Almagest, which described the geocentric model of the universe using deferents and epicycles. He worked in Alexandria around the second century. His model dominated astronomy for about fourteen centuries. For 10 points, name this scientist.

In this phenomenon, a massive object bends light from a distant background source, acting like a lens. Arthur Eddington's measurement during the 1919 solar eclipse confirmed Einstein's prediction of it. Astronomers use it to map dark matter in galaxy clusters. For 10 points, name this effect.

This is the largest moon of Neptune. Unusually, it orbits in the opposite direction to the planet's rotation, suggesting it was captured from the Kuiper Belt. Voyager 2 saw nitrogen geysers erupting on its surface in 1989. For 10 points, name this moon.

This dark gap about 4,800 kilometers wide separates Saturn's A and B rings. Its discoverer was an Italian-French astronomer in 1675, who also gives a name to a spacecraft that studied Saturn from 2004 to 2017. For 10 points, name this gap.

These stars brighten and dim with periods that correlate with their luminosity, a relation found in 1912 by a Harvard computer studying the Small Magellanic Cloud. They serve as standard candles for measuring distance. Delta Cephei is the prototype. For 10 points, name these pulsating variable stars.

A graduate student at Cambridge discovered the first of these objects in 1967 as a radio signal repeating about every 1.3 seconds. They are rapidly spinning neutron stars that sweep beams of radiation across space like a lighthouse. For 10 points, name these objects, whose first example was jokingly called LGM-1.

Maarten Schmidt identified the first of these in 1963 when he found that 3C 273 had a huge redshift. Powered by matter spiraling into a supermassive black hole, they are among the most luminous objects in the universe. For 10 points, name these "quasi-stellar" sources.

This is the maximum mass, about 1.4 solar masses, that a white dwarf can have without collapsing. It is named for an Indian-American astrophysicist who derived it in the early 1930s. Exceeding it triggers a Type Ia supernova. For 10 points, name this limit.

This radio source at the center of the Milky Way is a supermassive black hole of about four million solar masses. Stars such as S2 orbit it, and Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics for studying it. For 10 points, name this object in the constellation Sagittarius.

These are tightly bound, roughly spherical groups of hundreds of thousands of old stars orbiting in the galactic halo. Omega Centauri is the largest in the Milky Way, and Messier 13 is a famous one in Hercules. For 10 points, name these clusters, whose name suggests their shape.

This is the distance within which a moon held together only by its own gravity would be torn apart by tidal forces from its planet. Saturn's rings may lie within it. It is named for a nineteenth-century French astronomer. For 10 points, name this limit.
Answer these questions about moons.
parts: Which tiny moon of Saturn sprays plumes of water ice from its south pole?
Which moon of Jupiter is the most volcanically active body in the solar system?
Which large moon orbits Pluto at such a close distance that the two are often considered a double system?

parts: Which infrared space telescope, launched in 2021, is named for a NASA administrator of the Apollo era?
What type of telescope uses a large dish to collect radio waves, such as the Very Large Array?
What type of optical telescope, first built practically by Isaac Newton, uses a mirror as its main light collector?

parts: Which American astronomer discovered the period-luminosity relation for Cepheid variables?
Which British-American astronomer showed in her 1925 thesis that stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium?
Which American astronomer measured the rotation curves of galaxies and found evidence for dark matter?

q: Answer these questions about spacecraft and missions.
parts: Which 1970 Apollo mission suffered an oxygen tank explosion but returned safely to Earth?
Which first American space station was launched in 1973?
Which NASA probe, launched in 2006, flew past Pluto in 2015?

parts: Which constellation, named for a hunter, contains the stars Betelgeuse and Rigel?
Which constellation contains the Big Dipper asterism?
Which small constellation visible from the Southern Hemisphere is also called the Southern Cross?

q: Answer these questions about the origin of the universe.
parts: Which Belgian priest and physicist proposed in 1927 that the universe is expanding and later proposed a "primeval atom"?
Which English astronomer coined the phrase "Big Bang" on a radio program, although he favored a rival theory?
What name is given to the period of extremely rapid expansion in the early universe, proposed by Alan Guth?

q: Answer these questions about the formation of the solar system.
parts: What flat, rotating cloud of gas and dust around a young star gives rise to planets?
What process builds up larger bodies from smaller ones through collisions and gravity?
What is the name for the distance from the Sun beyond which water ice can survive, separating rocky and gas giant planets?

q: Answer these questions about the Moon.
parts: What name is given to the dark, smooth plains on the Moon formed by ancient lava flows?
What is the layer of loose, dusty rock covering the lunar surface?
The Moon always shows the same face to Earth because it is in what condition, in which its rotation period equals its orbital period?

q: This number is calculated from a Lorenz curve by comparing the area between the line of perfect equality and the actual curve to the total area beneath that line. The Italian statistician it is named for published it in 1912. A value of zero means everyone has the same income, while one means one person has everything. For 10 points, name this measure of income inequality.

Economists use the diamond-water paradox to illustrate this concept: water is far more useful than diamonds, yet much cheaper. The paradox is resolved by noting that price reflects the satisfaction gained from one additional unit rather than total satisfaction. Its value falls as consumption rises. For 10 points, name this concept, the extra satisfaction from one more unit of a good.

According to a popular story, Arthur Laffer drew this graph on a napkin in a Washington restaurant in the 1970s. It shows tax revenue rising with tax rates up to a point, then falling as rates approach one hundred percent. It was cited by supporters of supply-side economics in the Reagan administration. For 10 points, name this curve.

This effect describes how an initial injection of spending leads to a larger total change in income, because one person's spending becomes another's income. Its size is the reciprocal of one minus the marginal propensity to consume. Richard Kahn first described it, and Keynes popularized it. For 10 points, name this effect that magnifies changes in spending.

This New Zealand economist published a 1958 paper showing a historical inverse relationship between unemployment and wage growth in the United Kingdom. Paul Samuelson and Robert Solow later adapted it to inflation. It broke down in the 1970s. For 10 points, name this curve named after A. W. Phillips.

Pollution from a factory that harms nearby residents is an example of this kind of cost imposed on third parties who are not part of a transaction. Arthur Pigou proposed taxes to correct it. Ronald Coase argued that bargaining could sometimes resolve it. For 10 points, name this market failure, which can also be a positive spillover such as a neighbor's garden.

A lighthouse and national defense are standard examples of this kind of good, which is both nonrival and nonexcludable. Because people cannot be prevented from using it, private markets tend to underprovide it. For 10 points, name this category of good, usually paid for by taxes.

This problem arises when someone benefits from a good or service without paying for it, such as a person who watches public television during fundraising drives without donating. Mancur Olson analyzed it in The Logic of Collective Action. For 10 points, name this problem, which leads to underprovision of public goods.

Garrett Hardin popularized this phrase in a 1968 essay in Science, using the example of herders whose animals graze on shared pasture. Each herder gains from adding one more animal, but the pasture is eventually ruined. For 10 points, give this term for the overuse of a shared resource, which Elinor Ostrom later studied.

This economic doctrine dominated European thought from the sixteenth to the eighteenth centuries. It held that national wealth was measured by stocks of gold and silver, so a country should export more than it imports and acquire colonies. England's Navigation Acts followed it. For 10 points, name this doctrine, which Adam Smith criticized.

This English economist wrote On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation in 1817 and opposed the Corn Laws. He formulated the theory of rent and the idea that wages tend toward subsistence. A stockbroker before turning to economics, he developed a theory of trade using wine and cloth. For 10 points, name this economist.

This English clergyman published An Essay on the Principle of Population in 1798. He argued that population grows geometrically while food supply grows arithmetically, leading to famine and misery. For 10 points, name this man, whose pessimistic outlook earned economics the label of the dismal science.

This Austrian-born economist wrote The Road to Serfdom in 1944, warning that central planning leads to tyranny. He shared the 1974 Nobel Memorial Prize and debated Keynes. He taught at the London School of Economics and the University of Chicago. For 10 points, name this member of the Austrian school.

This Austrian-American economist popularized the phrase creative destruction in Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy in 1942. He argued that entrepreneurs and innovation drive growth by displacing old industries. He taught at Harvard. For 10 points, name this man.

A 1944 meeting at a resort in New Hampshire created the postwar international monetary order. Delegates from forty-four Allied nations established fixed exchange rates tied to the dollar, which was convertible to gold, and set up the International Monetary Fund. Keynes and Harry Dexter White were leading figures. For 10 points, name this conference or system, named for the resort town.

Under this system, a currency can be exchanged for a fixed amount of a precious metal. Franklin Roosevelt took the United States off of it domestically in 1933, and Richard Nixon ended dollar convertibility to it in 1971. Britain returned to it in 1925 under Winston Churchill. For 10 points, name this monetary system based on bullion.

This 1933 law, passed in response to bank failures, separated commercial banking from investment banking. It is named for a senator from Virginia and a representative from Alabama. Parts of it were repealed in 1999 by the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act. For 10 points, name this banking law.
This agency, created in 1933 and now insuring deposits up to a set limit, was meant to end bank runs. For 10 points, name this United States government corporation, abbreviated F-D-I-C.

Passed in 1890, this law was the first federal act to prohibit monopolies and trusts that restrain trade. It was used by Theodore Roosevelt's administration against the Northern Securities Company and against Standard Oil. For 10 points, name this antitrust law named for an Ohio senator.

Over one thousand economists signed a petition urging President Hoover to veto this 1930 law, which raised tariffs on over twenty thousand imported goods. Other countries retaliated, and world trade shrank. It is named for a senator from Utah and a representative from Oregon. For 10 points, name this tariff act.

In the 1630s, the prices of rare bulbs in the Dutch Republic soared to extraordinary levels before collapsing in 1637. Some single bulbs were reportedly worth more than a canal house. For 10 points, name this episode, often called the first speculative bubble, involving a flower.

OPEC is an example of this type of organization, in which producers agree to limit output and fix prices. Such agreements are illegal among competing firms in the United States. For 10 points, name this term for a group of producers acting together like a monopoly.

A water company or a local electric utility is often treated as this kind of firm, because very high fixed costs make it cheaper for one producer to serve the whole market. Governments typically regulate its prices instead of breaking it up. For 10 points, name this kind of monopoly that arises from cost structure rather than from conduct.

Airlines charging business travelers more than vacationers, and movie theaters offering student discounts, are examples of this practice. It requires that a seller have some market power and be able to keep buyers from reselling. For 10 points, name this practice of charging different prices to different buyers for the same product.

This concept explains why large factories often have lower cost per unit than small workshops. Spreading fixed costs over more output reduces average total cost, as in Henry Ford's assembly line. For 10 points, name this concept in which average cost falls as production increases.

In this market structure, there are many sellers of identical products, and no single firm can influence price, so each is a price taker. Wheat farming is often cited as an approximation. For 10 points, name this theoretical market structure, the opposite of monopoly.

On a graph, this curve slopes downward and shows the total quantity of goods and services demanded in an economy at each price level. It is the sum of consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports. For 10 points, name this macroeconomic concept, paired with aggregate supply.

Central banks use this kind of policy to control the money supply and interest rates. Examples include open market operations and changing the discount rate. For 10 points, name this kind of policy, distinguished from the fiscal kind that involves taxes and spending.

This British economist wrote Principles of Economics in 1890. He compared supply and demand to the blades of a pair of scissors and popularized the idea of consumer surplus. He taught at Cambridge, where he trained John Maynard Keynes. For 10 points, name this man.

A person who keeps watching a terrible movie because he already paid for the ticket is committing a fallacy involving this kind of cost. Economists say that this kind, which has already been spent and cannot be recovered, should not affect future decisions. For 10 points, name this kind of cost.

parts: In 2009, which American became the first woman to win the prize, for her work on how communities manage shared resources?
Which Indian economist won in 1998 for work on welfare economics and the causes of famine?
Which mathematician shared the 1994 prize for work on equilibrium in game theory and was the subject of the film A Beautiful Mind?

parts: What is the interest rate that a central bank charges commercial banks for short-term loans?
What term describes the central bank's buying and selling of government securities to adjust the money supply?
Which committee of the Federal Reserve, with twelve voting members, sets the target for the federal funds rate?

q: Answer these questions about taxes.
parts: What kind of tax takes a larger percentage of income from people who earn more?
What kind of tax takes a larger percentage of income from low earners than from high earners, such as a flat sales tax?
Which amendment, ratified in 1913, allowed Congress to levy an income tax without apportioning it among states?

parts: In which famous game do two suspects each decide whether to confess or stay silent, with the best joint result requiring cooperation?
What term names the outcome in which no player can gain by changing strategy alone?
Which Israeli-American psychologist won the 2002 prize for work with Amos Tversky on decisions under uncertainty?

Which 1907 financial crisis, ended partly through the efforts of J. P. Morgan, prompted calls to create a central bank in the United States?
At which Georgia island retreat did a secret meeting in 1910 draft the plan that led to the Federal Reserve Act?

q: Answer these questions about economic cycles.
parts: What term describes the repeating pattern of expansion and contraction of an economy?
Which private nonprofit group, based in Cambridge, Massachusetts, officially dates the beginning and end of United States recessions?
What name is given to the severe downturn that followed the collapse of the American housing market and the financial crisis of 2008?

q: Answer these questions about market structures.
parts: What term names a market with exactly two sellers?
What market structure, such as restaurants or clothing stores, has many sellers offering differentiated products?
Which index, abbreviated H-H-I, is calculated by summing the squares of firms' market shares and is used by regulators to measure market concentration?

q: In this task, subjects are shown the word green printed in red ink and must name the ink color rather than read the word. Reaction times are slower when the word and ink color conflict. John Ridley published it in 1935. For 10 points, name this effect, which demonstrates interference in attention.

A person who believes vaccines are dangerous and only reads articles supporting that belief shows this kind of bias. Peter Wason named it in the 1960s after card-selection experiments. For 10 points, name this tendency to seek out and favor information that agrees with what one already believes.

John B. Watson and Rosalie Rayner conducted this 1920 experiment at Johns Hopkins, in which a nine-month-old boy was conditioned to fear a white rat. The fear generalized to a rabbit and a fur coat. For 10 points, name this infamous study of conditioned emotional reactions.

This psychologist raised infant rhesus monkeys with two artificial mothers, one made of wire that gave milk and one covered in cloth. The babies clung to the cloth one. He worked at the University of Wisconsin. For 10 points, name this man whose experiments showed the importance of contact comfort.

This psychologist showed that the wording of questions can alter eyewitness memories. In her 1974 study with John Palmer, subjects estimated higher speeds when asked how fast cars smashed into each other. She also researched the lost in the mall technique. For 10 points, name this expert on false memories.

This Harvard psychologist proposed three levels of moral development, preconventional, conventional, and postconventional, and used the Heinz dilemma, in which a man steals a drug for his dying wife. For 10 points, name this man.

This Soviet psychologist, who died in 1934, argued that children learn through social interaction and defined a range of tasks that a child can do with help but not alone. For 10 points, name this author of Mind in Society, who coined the zone of proximal development.

In 1848, an iron rod blasted through this railroad foreman's skull in Vermont, destroying much of his left frontal lobe. His personality reportedly changed dramatically, though he lived for another twelve years. For 10 points, name this patient, whose case suggested a link between the brain and personality.

The patient Tan, who could say only that one syllable, led to the identification of this region in the left frontal lobe by a French physician in 1861. Damage to it causes a language disorder in which comprehension is intact but speech is halting. For 10 points, name this brain area, named for Paul.

Cutting this thick band of nerve fibers, as was done in some epilepsy patients, disconnects the two hemispheres of the brain. The patients can name objects in their right visual field but not their left. For 10 points, name this structure.

This American neuroscientist and Nobel laureate worked with Michael Gazzaniga on patients whose hemispheres had been separated. He showed that each hemisphere perceives things independently. His work won the 1981 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. For 10 points, name this split-brain researcher.

Using nonsense syllables like DAX and BOK, this German psychologist memorized lists to measure his own retention. In 1885 he published On Memory, showing that forgetting is rapid at first and then levels off. For 10 points, name this man who plotted the forgetting curve.

In 1964, a woman named Kitty Genovese was murdered in New York as bystanders reportedly did nothing. Researchers John Darley and Bibb Latane then showed that people are less likely to help when others are present. For 10 points, name this effect, named for those who watch.

When we see a driver cut us off, we tend to blame his bad character, but when we do the same we blame traffic. This bias, described by Lee Ross, is the tendency to overestimate personality and underestimate situation when explaining others' behavior. For 10 points, name this attribution bias.

Edward Thorndike coined this name for a tendency where one positive trait, such as attractiveness, causes people to assume other good traits in a person. For 10 points, give this term, which suggests a person is surrounded by a ring of light.

This American psychologist put hungry cats into puzzle boxes and measured how fast they learned to escape. His law of effect states that behaviors followed by satisfying consequences are strengthened. He taught at Columbia Teachers College. For 10 points, name this precursor of B. F. Skinner.

Max Wertheimer, Wolfgang Kohler, and Kurt Koffka founded this German school of psychology. Its slogan is that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. It studied perception, such as how we see a figure against a background. For 10 points, name this school, whose German name means shape.

This humanistic psychologist developed client-centered therapy and emphasized unconditional positive regard, empathy, and genuineness. He taught at the University of Chicago and wrote On Becoming a Person. For 10 points, name this man.
This Austrian psychiatrist broke with Freud in 1911 and founded individual psychology. He coined the term inferiority complex and emphasized birth order. For 10 points, name this man.

In this 1960s experiment at Stanford, researcher Walter Mischel offered young children a treat now or two if they waited. Later studies tracked the children's outcomes as adults. For 10 points, name this experiment on delayed gratification, which used a sweet.

This Harvard psychologist proposed eight types of intelligence, such as musical, spatial, and interpersonal, in his 1983 book Frames of Mind. For 10 points, name this man who developed the theory of multiple intelligences.

Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky identified three of these mental shortcuts, representativeness, availability, and anchoring. They let people make quick judgments but can lead to systematic errors. For 10 points, give this term for a rule of thumb used in decision making.

If asked whether the Mississippi River is longer than 500 miles and then asked its length, a person will give a lower estimate than if asked whether it is longer than 5,000 miles. For 10 points, name this cognitive bias in which an initial number influences later judgments.

The assassination of John F. Kennedy and the attacks of September 11 produced many of these detailed, vivid recollections of where one was when hearing the news. Roger Brown and James Kulik coined the term in 1977. For 10 points, name this kind of memory, which is not necessarily accurate.

When asked to recall a list of words, people remember the first and last items best. This pattern is the result of the primacy and recency effects. For 10 points, name this effect named for the order of items in a list.

This roughly twenty-four-hour cycle of sleeping and waking is controlled by the suprachiasmatic nucleus in the hypothalamus. Jet lag happens when it is disrupted. For 10 points, name this biological clock.

This effect is named for a Western Electric plant near Chicago, where productivity rose among workers whether lighting was increased or decreased. It suggests that people change behavior when they know they are being observed. For 10 points, name this effect.

This type of cell sends electrical and chemical messages in the nervous system. It has a cell body, dendrites, and an axon. Santiago Ramon y Cajal showed it was the basic unit of the brain. For 10 points, name this cell.

Parkinson's disease is linked to the loss of cells that produce this neurotransmitter in the substantia nigra, and it is also involved in the brain's reward system. Cocaine and other drugs boost its activity. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter.

What name is given to the tiny gap between two neurons where signals pass?
Which neurotransmitter, used at the junction between nerves and muscles, is depleted in patients with Alzheimer's disease?

What name is given to a committee that must approve research involving human subjects before it begins?

q: Answer these questions about therapies.
parts: What kind of therapy involves several clients meeting with a therapist together?
What technique for treating phobias gradually exposes patients to feared objects while they relax?
Which South African psychiatrist developed that technique in the 1950s?

q: Answer these questions about intelligence testing.
parts: Which French psychologist created the first practical intelligence test in 1905?
Which English psychologist proposed a general intelligence factor, called g?
Which British-American psychologist distinguished fluid from crystallized intelligence?

q: Answer these questions about sleep.
parts: What is the term for difficulty falling or staying asleep?
What disorder involves sudden attacks of sleep during the day?
Which hormone, produced by the pineal gland, helps regulate the sleep cycle?

q: Answer these questions about operant conditioning.
parts: What term describes giving a reward to increase the chance that a behavior is repeated?
Which reinforcement schedule, used in slot machines, gives rewards after an unpredictable number of responses?
What term describes rewarding successive approximations to teach a complex behavior?

q: Answer these questions about visual perception.
parts: What ability lets us judge how far away an object is?
Which apparatus, with a glass-covered drop, tested whether infants perceive depth?
Which two researchers, Eleanor Gibson and Richard Walk, built that apparatus at Cornell?

q: Cinematographer Gregg Toland used deep focus and low-angle shots with visible ceilings in this film. Its story is told through flashbacks as a reporter tries to learn the meaning of a dying man's final word, "Rosebud." Its protagonist is a newspaper tycoon modeled partly on William Randolph Hearst. For 10 points, name this 1941 film directed by and starring Orson Welles.

This director made the thrillers Vertigo and Rear Window, and he appeared in brief cameos in many of his own movies. A 1960 film of his features a murder in a shower at the Bates Motel. He was nicknamed the "Master of Suspense." For 10 points, name this British-born director of Psycho.

This director made a film about a great white shark terrorizing the beach town of Amity Island. He also directed a film in which a boy befriends a stranded alien who wants to phone home. He won Best Director Oscars for Schindler's List and Saving Private Ryan. For 10 points, name this director of Jaws and E.T.

In 1937 this man's studio released the first full-length cel-animated feature in English, based on a Brothers Grimm tale about a princess and seven dwarfs. His company later opened Disneyland in Anaheim in 1955. He voiced Mickey Mouse in early cartoons. For 10 points, name this American animator and founder of a namesake studio.

This franchise began in 1977 with a film in which Luke Skywalker joins a rebellion against the Galactic Empire. Its sound designer Ben Burtt created the breathing of Darth Vader and the voice of R2-D2. John Williams composed its famous theme. For 10 points, name this space-opera series created by George Lucas.

In this 1939 film, Judy Garland sings "Over the Rainbow" as Dorothy. The film switches from black-and-white to Technicolor when Dorothy opens her farmhouse door after a tornado. Dorothy travels the Yellow Brick Road with a Scarecrow, a Tin Man, and a Cowardly Lion. For 10 points, name this film based on a book by L. Frank Baum.

Directed by John Lasseter, this 1995 film was the first feature-length movie made entirely with computer animation. Its songs were written by Randy Newman, including "You've Got a Friend in Me." Its plot concerns a cowboy doll who is jealous of a new space ranger action figure named Buzz Lightyear. For 10 points, name this first Pixar feature.

This photographer co-founded Group f/64 and developed the Zone System for controlling exposure and contrast. He is famous for black-and-white landscapes such as Moonrise, Hernandez, New Mexico. His many images of Half Dome made Yosemite National Park iconic. For 10 points, name this American photographer.

This silent film star created a character with a bowler hat, a toothbrush mustache, a cane, and baggy pants, known as the Tramp. He directed and starred in The Gold Rush and Modern Times. He co-founded United Artists in 1919. For 10 points, name this British-born comedian.

This director's film Princess Mononoke features a prince who fights a curse and the spirits of the forest. He co-founded Studio Ghibli, and his film about a girl named Chihiro who works in a bathhouse for spirits won an Oscar for Best Animated Feature. For 10 points, name this Japanese director of Spirited Away.

This Japanese director's Rashomon retells one crime from conflicting points of view. His film about villagers who hire ronin to defend them from bandits inspired the Western The Magnificent Seven. He frequently cast Toshiro Mifune. For 10 points, name this director of Seven Samurai.

This photographer worked for the Farm Security Administration during the Great Depression. In 1936 she photographed a worried pea-picker and her children in Nipomo, California. That image became the iconic Migrant Mother. For 10 points, name this American documentary photographer.

This 1927 German silent film features a robot double of a woman named Maria who incites workers to riot. It depicts a futuristic city with a wealthy upper class living above underground laborers. It was directed by Fritz Lang. For 10 points, name this expressionist science-fiction classic.

In this 1952 musical, a silent-film star played by Gene Kelly dances in a downpour and splashes through puddles while swinging a lamppost. Donald O'Connor performs "Make 'Em Laugh" in it, and Debbie Reynolds co-stars. The plot concerns Hollywood's transition to talking pictures. For 10 points, name this classic musical named for a weather activity.

In this 1972 film, Marlon Brando plays Vito Corleone, the head of a New York crime family. An offer that "can't be refused" and a horse's head in a bed are famous moments. Al Pacino plays the son Michael. For 10 points, name this film directed by Francis Ford Coppola from a novel by Mario Puzo.

In 1839 the French government announced the invention of this process, which produced a unique image on a silvered copper plate exposed to iodine vapor and developed with mercury fumes. It was developed by Joseph Nicephore Niepce's partner. For 10 points, name this early photographic process named for Louis Daguerre.

This director's film 2001: A Space Odyssey features the computer HAL 9000. He also directed A Clockwork Orange and filmed Jack Nicholson in The Shining. He was known for perfectionism and symmetrical one-point-perspective shots. For 10 points, name this American director.

This silent comedian, nicknamed "The Great Stone Face," performed his own dangerous stunts. In a film set in the American Civil War, he plays a train engineer chasing a stolen locomotive named The General. In Steamboat Bill, Jr., a house front falls around him. For 10 points, name this rival of Charlie Chaplin.

This composer wrote the scores for Jaws, Raiders of the Lost Ark, and the Harry Potter films. Two notes alternating in a menacing pattern represent the shark in one score. He has also conducted the Boston Pops. For 10 points, name this American film composer who wrote the Star Wars theme.

This 1927 film starring Al Jolson is often considered the first feature with synchronized spoken dialogue and songs. It was produced by Warner Bros. using the Vitaphone sound-on-disc system. Jolson sings "Mammy" in it. For 10 points, name this film whose title describes a vocalist.

This 1942 film is set in Morocco, where nightclub owner Rick Blaine meets his former love Ilsa Lund. Humphrey Bogart stars in it, and Dooley Wilson plays "As Time Goes By." It features the line "Here's looking at you, kid." For 10 points, name this film set in a city on the Atlantic coast of Africa, directed by Michael Curtiz.

This puppeteer created Kermit the Frog and the Muppets. He also helped create Sesame Street characters such as Big Bird's pals Bert and Ernie. He directed the fantasy films The Dark Crystal and Labyrinth. For 10 points, name this American puppeteer.

This cartoon character first appeared in the 1928 short Steamboat Willie, which featured synchronized sound. He wears red shorts with white buttons and has a girlfriend named Minnie. He is voiced in early cartoons by his creator. For 10 points, name this cartoon mouse who is the mascot of Disney.

In December 1895 in the basement of the Grand Cafe in Paris, two brothers held one of the first public paid screenings of projected films. They patented the Cinematographe, which both filmed and projected. Their short films include Workers Leaving the Factory. For 10 points, give the surname shared by these French inventors.

This French magician-turned-filmmaker pioneered special effects such as the stop trick and double exposure. His 1902 film shows a bullet-shaped capsule landing in the eye of the face of the Man in the Moon. For 10 points, name this director of A Trip to the Moon.

This Soviet director's film Battleship Potemkin includes a massacre on the Odessa Steps with a baby carriage rolling down. He wrote about using montage to create meaning by juxtaposing shots. His other films include Strike and October. For 10 points, name this Russian director.

This director made the films Taxi Driver and Raging Bull, both starring Robert De Niro. He won his first Best Director Oscar for The Departed. He often collaborates with editor Thelma Schoonmaker and has made many films about the mob, like Goodfellas. For 10 points, name this American director.

This writer created an anthology series that begins with a narration about a "fifth dimension" and often ends with a twist. Its episodes included "Time Enough at Last," about a bookworm who breaks his glasses, and "To Serve Man." He also hosted it on CBS beginning in 1959. For 10 points, name this creator of The Twilight Zone.

In the 1870s this English-born photographer working for Leland Stanford used a row of cameras with trip wires to capture a galloping horse in sequential frames. His work settled whether all four hooves leave the ground. He later invented the zoopraxiscope. For 10 points, name this pioneer of motion photography.

In animation, this is a sequence of small drawings or sketches laid out like a comic strip to plan a film shot by shot. Artists at the Disney studio popularized it in the 1930s. Directors use it before filming to plan camera angles and action. For 10 points, name this planning tool whose name suggests a place where tales are kept.

q: This structure was built for the 1889 World's Fair, which marked the centennial of the French Revolution. Its wrought-iron lattice design was criticized by some Parisian artists when it was proposed. It was designed by the firm of an engineer who also built the framework of the Statue of Liberty. For 10 points, name this Paris landmark named for Gustave.

This temple on the Acropolis was dedicated to the goddess Athena and built under Pericles in the fifth century BC. Its architects were Ictinus and Callicrates, and Phidias oversaw its sculpture. Its frieze was partly removed by Lord Elgin. For 10 points, name this Doric temple in Athens.

This architect founded the Prairie School and designed homes with low horizontal lines, such as the Robie House in Chicago. He designed his own studios, Taliesin in Wisconsin and Taliesin West in Arizona. He championed "organic architecture." For 10 points, name this American architect of Fallingwater.

This amphitheater in Rome was built under the Flavian emperors and could seat roughly fifty thousand spectators. Its arena once hosted gladiator fights and mock hunts. Its exterior uses stacked arches framed by Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian columns. For 10 points, name this large Roman ruin.

This Roman building's dome is made of concrete and was the largest in the world for many centuries. A circular opening at the top of the dome, called an oculus, lets in light and rain. It was built under Hadrian and later became a church that houses the tomb of the painter Raphael. For 10 points, name this temple to all gods in Rome.

This mausoleum in Agra was built by Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. It is made of white marble, with four minarets framing a central dome and a long reflecting pool in front. It was completed in the seventeenth century. For 10 points, name this Mughal monument in India.

This style of European architecture succeeded the Romanesque and is characterized by pointed arches, ribbed vaults, and large stained-glass windows. It began at the Abbey of Saint-Denis under Abbot Suger. Chartres and Reims are cathedrals in this style. For 10 points, name this medieval style, whose name is now also applied to a type of dark subculture.

Used on cathedrals like Notre-Dame, these exterior arched supports transfer the thrust of a high stone vault outward to piers. They allowed walls to be thin and filled with stained glass. The name describes how they appear to hover in the air. For 10 points, name these architectural supports in Gothic cathedrals.

This architect made his own Santa Monica house from chain-link fencing and corrugated metal. He designed the Dancing House in Prague with Vlado Milunic and the Experience Music Project in Seattle. His Los Angeles concert hall for the Philharmonic has stainless-steel curves. For 10 points, name this Canadian-American deconstructivist architect.

This Frank Lloyd Wright house was built in Pennsylvania for the Kaufmann family. Cantilevered concrete terraces extend over a waterfall on Bear Run. It blends into its wooded setting. For 10 points, name this house built over a stream, whose name describes cascading water.

Completed in 1973, this building in Sydney Harbour has a roof of white ceramic-tiled shells resembling sails. Its Danish architect, Jorn Utzon, resigned from the project before it was finished. It hosts opera and concerts. For 10 points, name this Australian landmark.

This sixth-century Byzantine church in Constantinople was built under Emperor Justinian with a huge central dome supported by pendentives. Its architects were Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus. After 1453 it became a mosque and minarets were added. For 10 points, name this building in Istanbul whose name means "Holy Wisdom."

Construction on this cathedral on the Île de la Cité began in 1163 under Bishop Maurice de Sully. It has rose windows and a spire built by Viollet-le-Duc after a prior spire was removed. A Victor Hugo novel features its hunchbacked bell ringer. For 10 points, name this Paris cathedral damaged by fire in 2019.

This Greek column style has a bell-shaped capital decorated with acanthus leaves. It is the most ornate of the three classical orders. It was popular with the Romans and is named for a Greek city. For 10 points, name this order, which follows the Doric and Ionic.

The oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and the only one still largely standing, this tomb was built for the pharaoh Khufu. It was originally covered in smooth white limestone casing. Its sides rise to a point above the Giza plateau. For 10 points, name this largest of the ancient Egyptian pyramids.

This architect designed the Wainwright Building in Saint Louis and the Carson Pirie Scott store in Chicago. He is credited with the maxim "form ever follows function." He was the early employer and mentor of Frank Lloyd Wright. For 10 points, name this "father of skyscrapers" from Chicago.

This Florentine architect won the competition to complete a cathedral by building a double-shelled octagonal dome without wooden centering. He also designed the Ospedale degli Innocenti and the Pazzi Chapel. He studied Roman ruins and helped develop linear perspective. For 10 points, name this Renaissance architect of the dome of the Florence Cathedral.

This Swiss-French architect designed Villa Savoye, which stands on pilotis and has a roof garden. His "five points of architecture" were widely influential, and he envisioned a "Radiant City." He also designed the chapel at Ronchamp. For 10 points, name this pioneer of modernism, who called a house "a machine for living in."

This German-born architect directed the Bauhaus before moving to Chicago. He designed the Seagram Building in New York and the Farnsworth House. He is associated with the maxim "less is more." For 10 points, name this modernist whose name includes "van der Rohe."

Built in 1931 in just over a year, this New York Art Deco skyscraper stood as the tallest building for about forty years. It was designed by Shreve, Lamb and Harmon. The King Kong film shows the ape climbing it. For 10 points, name this Manhattan landmark on Fifth Avenue named for the state's nickname.

This monument in Washington, D.C. is a marble obelisk designed by Robert Mills. Construction paused for years during the 1850s, and a visible change in marble color marks that gap. It was dedicated in the 1880s to honor the first president. For 10 points, name this 555-foot tall landmark on the National Mall.

After the Great Fire of London in 1666, this architect rebuilt dozens of churches and designed a domed cathedral on Ludgate Hill. His Royal Observatory at Greenwich also dates from his career. He was also an astronomer and mathematician. For 10 points, name this man who designed Saint Paul's Cathedral.

In an arch, this wedge-shaped stone at the top locks the other pieces in place. Removing it would cause the arch to collapse. The term is used figuratively for the central supporting element of an idea. For 10 points, name this stone at the crown of an arch.

This basilica in Barcelona has been under construction since 1882 and features towers meant to symbolize the apostles and evangelists. Its Nativity Facade is lavishly sculpted. Its architect was killed by a tram in 1926. For 10 points, name this Catalan church, whose name means "Holy Family."

This Catalan Modernista architect designed the mosaic-covered park known as Park Guell. He also created Casa Batllo and Casa Mila, nicknamed La Pedrera. His buildings use curving, organic forms inspired by nature. For 10 points, name this architect of the Sagrada Familia.

Founded by Walter Gropius in Weimar in 1919, this German school combined fine arts and crafts and promoted functional design. It moved to Dessau and its building there has a glass curtain wall. The Nazis closed it in 1933. For 10 points, name this influential design school.

This New York skyscraper designed by William Van Alen was briefly the world's tallest building. Its crown is a stainless-steel spire with sunburst arches, and its corners have eagle gargoyles modeled on car hood ornaments. It was built for an automobile company. For 10 points, name this Art Deco skyscraper.

This palace-fortress above Granada was built by the Nasrid dynasty. It is known for the Court of the Lions, with its fountain and slender columns, and its muqarnas ceilings and geometric tilework. For 10 points, name this Moorish complex in southern Spain whose name means "the red one."

This royal palace near Paris was expanded by Louis XIV, who moved the court there in 1682. Its Hall of Mirrors was the site of the proclamation of the German Empire in 1871 and of a 1919 peace treaty. Its gardens were designed by Andre Le Notre. For 10 points, name this French palace.

This prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in England consists of large standing stones arranged in a circle with horizontal lintels. Its larger sarsen stones weigh many tons. It is aligned with the summer solstice sunrise. For 10 points, name this Neolithic site in Wiltshire.
